title: Best Start in Life, one year on: what's actually landed
excerpt: A look at what's changed — and what hasn't — a year into supporting local Best Start in Life delivery, from operational plans to Healthy Babies pathways.
coverAlt: A young boy wearing glasses builds a tower out of toy blocks
body: National policy intent around Best Start in Life has been consistent for several years now. What varies enormously is how far that intent has actually translated into different day-to-day experiences for babies, children and families on the ground — and that gap is where most of our critical-friend work sits.

A year into supporting several local areas through their BSIL operational plans and Healthy Babies integrated pathways, a few things stand out. The areas making the most visible progress aren't necessarily the best-resourced ones — they're the ones that treated the plan as a live operating document rather than a submission exercise, with named ownership and a genuine test-and-learn cycle behind it.

The second pattern is about join-up. Health visiting, early years settings, family hubs and VCS partners each hold a piece of a child's early experience, but the system rarely asks any single person to hold the whole picture. Where that role has been created — even informally — services report catching more issues earlier and duplicating less effort.

None of this is a finished story. But it's evidence that the difference between a strategy and a lived reality is mostly about follow-through, ownership and honest review — not about writing a better plan in the first place.
